title: Circulation: Heart & Blood (Extended)
description: Single and double circulation, heart valves and wall thickness, the heartbeat sequence and exercise, blood vessel structure, the hepatic vessels, white blood cells and clotting — the Extended tier of IGCSE Biology 0610.

notes.heading: Single and Double Circulation
notes.body:
📌 Definitions
• **Single circulation** (a fish): blood passes through the heart **once** in each complete circuit — heart → gills → body → heart.
• **Double circulation** (a mammal): blood passes through the heart **twice** in each complete circuit — a **pulmonary** loop (heart → lungs → heart) and a **systemic** loop (heart → body → heart).

🔑 The two advantages of double circulation (the standard 2-mark answer)
1. Blood is **pumped again** after picking up oxygen in the lungs, so it reaches the body tissues at **higher pressure** and flows faster — more oxygen and glucose delivered per second. (In a fish, pressure is lost as blood squeezes through the gill capillaries, so the body receives a slow, low-pressure supply.)
2. Oxygenated and deoxygenated blood are **kept completely separate**, so the tissues receive fully oxygenated blood.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Drawing the mammalian circuit as one big circle. The lungs sit BETWEEN the body's return and the body's supply — blood MUST pass through the heart twice per circuit.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Fish: one pump, one loop, pressure lost at the gills.
• Mammal: two loops; the second pump restores pressure and prevents mixing.

illustration.alt: Two circulation diagrams side by side: a fish single circulation (heart to gills to body and back to the heart) and a mammal double circulation with separate pulmonary and systemic loops through one heart.
illustration.caption: Red = oxygenated blood, blue = deoxygenated. The mammalian heart pumps the blood twice per circuit, keeping body pressure high and the two bloods separate.

notes.heading: Heart Valves: One-Way Doors
notes.body:
📌 The two sets you must identify on a heart diagram
• **Atrioventricular (AV) valves** — between each atrium and its ventricle (the tricuspid valve on the right, the bicuspid valve on the left).
• **Semilunar valves** — at the bases of the two arteries leaving the heart: the **aorta** and the **pulmonary artery**.

🔑 What they do
Valves keep blood flowing in **one direction only** by preventing backflow:
• AV valves stop blood flowing back into the **atria** when the ventricles contract.
• Semilunar valves stop blood flowing back into the **ventricles** from the arteries when the ventricles relax.

🔑 How they do it
Blood flowing the correct way pushes a valve OPEN; the moment blood starts to flow backwards, the valve cusps fill and slam SHUT. Pressure behind a valve closes it; pressure in front of it opens it.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Placing valves 'in the septum' or between the two ventricles. Heart valves sit only at the atrium–ventricle junctions and at the artery exits. (The valves inside VEINS are a separate set — see the blood vessels note.)

📎 Key Points to Remember
• AV valves: between atrium and ventricle. Semilunar valves: base of aorta and pulmonary artery.
• A valve answer = 'prevents backflow' + state WHERE the blood would flow back to.

notes.heading: Wall Thickness and the Septum
notes.body:
🔑 Left ventricle vs right ventricle
The **left ventricle has a thicker muscular wall than the right** because it must pump blood at **high pressure around the whole body** (the systemic circuit). The right ventricle pumps only to the **nearby lungs** — a short, low-resistance circuit; high pressure there would damage the delicate lung capillaries.

🔑 Atria vs ventricles
The **atria have thinner walls than the ventricles** because they only push blood the **short distance into the ventricles below** — much of the filling happens passively as the ventricles relax.

🔑 The septum
The **septum** is the wall separating the left and right sides of the heart. It keeps **oxygenated blood (left side) fully separate from deoxygenated blood (right side)**, so the body is supplied with blood carrying the maximum possible oxygen. A hole in the septum lets the two mix and reduces oxygen delivery.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Explaining wall thickness by the VOLUME of blood pumped — both ventricles pump the same volume per beat. The difference is the DISTANCE and PRESSURE of the circuit each one supplies.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Wall thickness matches workload: left ventricle thickest, right ventricle next, atria thinnest.
• Septum = no mixing = fully oxygenated blood to the body.

notes.heading: The Heartbeat Sequence and Exercise
notes.body:
🔑 One heartbeat, in order
1. The **atria contract** → blood is pushed through the open **AV valves** into the ventricles.
2. The **ventricles contract** → the **AV valves snap shut** (stopping backflow into the atria) and the rising pressure forces the **semilunar valves open** → blood is ejected into the **aorta and pulmonary artery**.
3. The heart muscle **relaxes** → the **semilunar valves close** (stopping backflow from the arteries) and the atria refill with blood from the veins.

🔑 Physical activity and heart rate
During exercise the muscles respire faster, so the **heart rate increases** to:
• deliver **oxygen and glucose** to the muscles faster, and
• remove **carbon dioxide** faster.
After exercise the heart rate falls back during recovery; a fitter heart returns to its resting rate sooner.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing 'the valves open when the heart contracts' without saying which chamber contracts and which valve responds. Always state: atria contract → AV valves OPEN; ventricles contract → AV valves CLOSE and semilunar valves OPEN.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Atria contract → ventricles contract → relax; valves open and close in response to pressure changes.
• Exercise → higher heart rate → faster O₂ and glucose delivery, faster CO₂ removal.

notes.heading: Arteries, Veins and Capillaries: Structure Matches Pressure
notes.body:
🔑 Arteries (carry blood AWAY from the heart)
Blood arrives at **high pressure** in pulses straight from the ventricles → arteries have **thick walls containing elastic fibres and muscle** and a **narrow lumen**. The elastic wall stretches with each pulse and recoils between beats, smoothing the flow.

🔑 Veins (carry blood BACK to the heart)
Pressure has been lost in the capillaries, so blood flows **slowly at low pressure** → veins have **thin walls** (little muscle or elastic tissue), a **wide lumen** (low resistance) and **valves** to prevent backflow; the squeezing of surrounding skeletal muscles helps push blood along.

🔑 Capillaries
Capillaries link arteries to veins within the tissues. Their walls are **one cell thick**, giving a **short diffusion distance** so oxygen, glucose, carbon dioxide and wastes exchange quickly between blood and cells; the tiny lumen slows the blood, leaving time for exchange.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Saying arteries 'carry oxygenated blood'. The pulmonary artery carries DEoxygenated blood. Define vessels by DIRECTION — arteries carry blood away from the heart, veins carry it back.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• High pressure → thick elastic, muscular wall, narrow lumen (artery); low pressure → thin wall, wide lumen, valves (vein).
• Capillary = a wall one cell thick, for rapid exchange.

notes.heading: The Hepatic Vessels
notes.body:
📌 Three named vessels serve the liver
• **Hepatic artery** — a branch of the aorta carrying **oxygenated blood TO the liver** (the liver's own oxygen supply).
• **Hepatic vein** — carries **deoxygenated blood FROM the liver** to the vena cava.
• **Hepatic portal vein** — carries **deoxygenated blood rich in digested food** (e.g. glucose and amino acids) **from the small intestine TO the liver**.

🔑 Why the portal vein is special
An ordinary vein returns blood straight to the heart; the hepatic portal vein instead connects the capillaries of the intestine to a SECOND capillary network inside the liver. The liver can then process the absorbed food molecules (for example storing glucose as glycogen) before the blood rejoins the general circulation.

🔑 What the examiner wants
On a diagram, identify each vessel from its DIRECTION and CONTENTS: towards the liver carrying digested food = hepatic portal vein; away from the liver = hepatic vein; towards the liver from the aorta with oxygenated blood = hepatic artery.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Calling the hepatic portal vein an artery 'because it carries blood to an organ'. Vessel names follow the connection to the HEART — arteries leave it, veins return towards it; a vessel joining two organs' capillary networks is a (portal) vein.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Hepatic artery: in, with oxygen. Hepatic vein: out, deoxygenated. Hepatic portal vein: in, from the intestine, rich in digested food.

notes.heading: White Blood Cells and Clotting
notes.body:
📌 The two white blood cells you must identify (e.g. on a blood micrograph)
• **Lymphocytes** — smaller cells with a **large, round nucleus** filling most of the cell; they **produce antibodies** — proteins that bind to specific pathogens, clumping them or marking them for destruction.
• **Phagocytes** — larger cells, often with a **lobed nucleus**; they **engulf and digest pathogens** (the process is phagocytosis).

🔑 Comparing their roles for 'distinguish' questions
Lymphocytes = chemical defence (antibodies against a SPECIFIC pathogen); phagocytes = physical defence (engulfing any pathogen). Tie 'produces antibodies' to LYMPHOCYTES only — that is where the mark is.

🔑 Blood clotting — the sequence
1. Damage to a blood vessel triggers the clotting response (platelets are involved at this step).
2. The soluble plasma protein **fibrinogen is converted to insoluble fibrin**.
3. Fibrin forms a **mesh of fibres** that traps red blood cells → a **clot** (which dries as a scab), preventing further blood loss and stopping pathogens entering the wound.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing that red blood cells or platelets 'turn into fibrin'. The conversion is **fibrinogen → fibrin**; the fibrin mesh does the trapping.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Lymphocyte → produces antibodies; phagocyte → engulfs and digests pathogens.
• Clotting: fibrinogen → fibrin mesh → traps cells → clot.

flashcards.definition: The fish circulation pattern: blood passes through the heart once per circuit — heart → gills → body → heart.
flashcards.example: In a fish, pressure is lost in the gill capillaries, so the body gets a low-pressure supply.

flashcards.definition: The mammal circulation pattern: blood passes through the heart twice per circuit — a pulmonary loop (heart–lungs–heart) and a systemic loop (heart–body–heart).
flashcards.example: A human's blood is pumped to the lungs, returns to the heart, and is pumped again to the body.

flashcards.definition: A valve between an atrium and its ventricle; it prevents blood flowing back into the atrium when the ventricle contracts.
flashcards.example: The tricuspid (right) and bicuspid (left) valves are the atrioventricular valves.

flashcards.definition: A valve at the base of the aorta or pulmonary artery; it prevents blood flowing back into the ventricles when they relax.
flashcards.example: When the ventricles relax, the semilunar valves snap shut so arterial blood cannot fall back in.

flashcards.definition: The wall separating the left and right sides of the heart, keeping oxygenated and deoxygenated blood apart.
flashcards.example: An intact septum means the body receives fully oxygenated blood from the left side.

flashcards.definition: Thick wall with elastic fibres and muscle, narrow lumen — suited to carrying blood away from the heart at high pressure, smoothing the pulses.
flashcards.example: The aorta stretches with each heartbeat and recoils between beats.

flashcards.definition: Thin wall, wide lumen and valves — suited to carrying blood back to the heart at low pressure.
flashcards.example: Leg veins use valves plus the squeeze of skeletal muscles to return blood upward.

flashcards.definition: A vessel with a wall one cell thick, giving a short diffusion distance for exchange of materials between blood and tissues.
flashcards.example: Oxygen and glucose diffuse out of capillaries into muscle cells during exercise.

flashcards.definition: The vessel carrying deoxygenated blood rich in digested food from the small intestine to the liver.
flashcards.example: After a meal, absorbed glucose travels to the liver in the hepatic portal vein.

flashcards.definition: A white blood cell (large round nucleus) that produces antibodies against specific pathogens.
flashcards.example: Lymphocytes release antibodies that bind to bacteria and mark them for destruction.

flashcards.definition: A white blood cell (often with a lobed nucleus) that engulfs and digests pathogens.
flashcards.example: Phagocytes surround and ingest bacteria at an infected cut.

flashcards.definition: In clotting, soluble fibrinogen is converted to insoluble fibrin, which forms a mesh trapping blood cells to form a clot.
flashcards.example: At a wound, fibrin fibres trap red blood cells, forming a clot that dries as a scab.

questions.stem: Which sequence shows the single circulation of a fish?
choices: Heart → lungs → body → heart
Heart → body → lungs → heart
Heart → gills → body → heart
Gills → heart → body → lungs
questions.explanation: A fish has no lungs: the heart pumps blood to the gills (where it picks up oxygen), then straight on to the body, and back to the heart — one pass through the heart per circuit. Any route mentioning lungs describes a mammal.

questions.stem: What is an advantage of the mammalian double circulation over the fish single circulation?
choices: Blood is pumped again after picking up oxygen in the lungs, so it reaches the body at higher pressure
Blood passes through the heart only once, saving energy
Oxygenated and deoxygenated blood mix in the heart, speeding up the flow
The heart can beat more slowly because the circuit is shorter
questions.explanation: In the double circulation the blood returns to the heart after the lungs and is re-pressurised before going to the body — faster delivery of oxygen and glucose. In a fish, pressure is lost in the gill capillaries, so the body supply is slow and low-pressure.

questions.stem: Where are the atrioventricular valves found?
choices: At the base of the aorta
Between the atria and the ventricles
Inside the veins of the legs
In the septum between the two sides of the heart
questions.explanation: Atrioventricular valves sit at the junction of each atrium and ventricle (tricuspid right, bicuspid left). Valves at the base of the aorta are semilunar valves, and the septum is a solid wall with no valves.

questions.stem: What is the function of the semilunar valves?
choices: To prevent blood flowing back from the ventricles into the atria
To separate oxygenated blood from deoxygenated blood
To control the heart rate
To prevent blood flowing back into the ventricles from the aorta and pulmonary artery
questions.explanation: Semilunar valves sit at the exits of the ventricles (base of aorta and pulmonary artery) and close when the ventricles relax, stopping arterial blood falling back in. Backflow into the ATRIA is prevented by the atrioventricular valves — the classic swap.

questions.stem: Why is the wall of the left ventricle thicker than the wall of the right ventricle?
choices: It must pump blood at higher pressure around the whole body, while the right ventricle pumps only to the nearby lungs
It pumps blood to the lungs, which offer high resistance
It receives blood at high pressure directly from the vena cava
It contains a greater volume of blood than the right ventricle
questions.explanation: The left ventricle supplies the whole-body systemic circuit, which is long and high-resistance, so it needs thick muscle to generate high pressure. The right ventricle supplies the short lung circuit — and both ventricles pump the SAME volume per beat, so volume is not the reason.

questions.stem: Why are the walls of the atria thinner than the walls of the ventricles?
choices: The atria contain valves that do the pumping for them
The atria receive blood rather than pumping it anywhere
The atria only need to push blood the short distance down into the ventricles
The atria hold a smaller volume of blood than the ventricles
questions.explanation: Wall thickness matches workload: the atria pump blood only into the ventricles just below them (and much of the filling is passive), so little muscle is needed. The ventricles must eject blood to the lungs and the whole body, so they need thick walls.

questions.stem: Why is the septum important for the heart's function?
choices: It produces the electrical signal for the heartbeat
It prevents oxygenated and deoxygenated blood mixing, so the body receives fully oxygenated blood
It anchors the heart valves in place
It slows the flow of blood through the heart
questions.explanation: The septum divides the heart's right (deoxygenated) and left (oxygenated) sides. Complete separation means the blood pumped to the body carries the maximum oxygen — a hole in the septum lets the two mix and reduces oxygen delivery.

questions.stem: During one heartbeat, which sequence of events is correct?
choices: Ventricles contract → AV valves open → blood enters the atria
Atria contract → semilunar valves open → blood enters the arteries
Ventricles relax → AV valves close → semilunar valves open
Atria contract → AV valves open and the ventricles fill → ventricles contract → AV valves close and semilunar valves open → blood is ejected into the arteries
questions.explanation: The correct order is: atria contract pushing blood through the open AV valves; then ventricles contract, which snaps the AV valves SHUT and forces the semilunar valves OPEN, ejecting blood into the aorta and pulmonary artery. The other options pair the wrong chamber contraction with the wrong valve response.

questions.stem: Why does the heart rate increase during physical activity?
choices: To deliver oxygen and glucose to the muscles and remove carbon dioxide faster
To reduce the blood pressure in the arteries
To warm the muscles by friction of the flowing blood
Because the valves in the leg veins block the returning blood
questions.explanation: Working muscles respire faster, so they need oxygen and glucose delivered more quickly and the extra carbon dioxide removed more quickly — a faster heart rate circulates the blood faster. Heart rate changes do not reduce arterial pressure.

questions.stem: How is an artery's structure related to the pressure of the blood it carries?
choices: Its thin wall allows substances to diffuse out quickly
Its wide lumen and valves prevent backflow at low pressure
Its thick elastic and muscular wall withstands the high-pressure pulses from the ventricles and smooths the flow
Its one-cell-thick wall speeds up exchange with the tissues
questions.explanation: Arteries carry blood at high pressure in pulses, so they have thick elastic muscular walls (stretch and recoil) with a narrow lumen. Thin walls and valves describe veins; a one-cell-thick wall describes a capillary.

questions.stem: Capillaries are adapted for exchanging materials with the tissues because their walls:
choices: are thick and muscular
are one cell thick, giving a short diffusion distance
contain valves to direct the flow
are elastic, smoothing the pulse
questions.explanation: A wall one cell thick gives the shortest possible diffusion distance, so oxygen, glucose, carbon dioxide and wastes cross quickly between blood and cells. Thick walls and elasticity are artery features; valves are a vein feature.

questions.stem: A blood vessel carries deoxygenated blood rich in digested food molecules from the small intestine to the liver. Which vessel is it?
choices: Hepatic artery
Hepatic vein
Renal vein
Hepatic portal vein
questions.explanation: The hepatic portal vein runs from the intestine's capillaries to the liver's capillaries, carrying absorbed food molecules for processing. The hepatic artery brings oxygenated blood from the aorta; the hepatic vein carries blood AWAY from the liver; the renal vein serves the kidney.

choices: Lymphocytes
Phagocytes
Red blood cells
Platelets
questions.explanation: Lymphocytes produce antibodies against specific pathogens. Phagocytes defend by engulfing and digesting pathogens instead; red blood cells carry oxygen and platelets are involved in clotting.

questions.stem: How do phagocytes defend the body against disease?
choices: By producing antibodies that bind to pathogens
By converting fibrinogen to fibrin
By engulfing and digesting pathogens
By carrying oxygen to infected tissue
questions.explanation: Phagocytes surround, engulf and digest pathogens (phagocytosis). Antibody production is the role of lymphocytes, and fibrinogen conversion is part of clotting — two classic swaps in this topic.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes blood clotting?
choices: Platelets dissolve to form fibrin directly at the wound
Soluble fibrinogen is converted to insoluble fibrin, which forms a mesh that traps blood cells
Red blood cells release fibrinogen when they reach a wound
Antibodies stick the edges of the wound together
questions.explanation: Clotting converts the soluble plasma protein fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin fibres; the fibrin mesh traps red blood cells and platelets to form the clot. Platelets trigger the process but do not themselves become fibrin, and antibodies fight pathogens, not blood loss.
